title: Power Earnings Gap
teaches: The Power Earnings Gap as we trade it: an established leader in a base or a quiet uptrend reports a quarter the market did not expect and gaps up on heavy volume; the gap day closes strong with the gap still open; we buy as price trades over the first orderly pause high with a market order, the stop sits a few cents under the pause or trigger-day low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the 10-day or 21-day trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

walkthroughs.title: AMZN, October 2017: the classic pause buy
steps: AMZN, 2017. A five-month base, then a report after the close on 2017-10-26. So 2017-10-27 is the PEG day.
The gap is 6 ATRs on 5.5x volume, closing at 0.92 of its range. The pause: five days, 1.7% deep.
Buy at market over the pause high, 56.14. Stop a few cents under the low, 55.39.
Failure mode: the gap fills, or a close under the gap-day low. Instead 3R came in 13 sessions. Sell into the push.

walkthroughs.title: BIDU, February 2010: a flat shelf and two tight days
steps: BIDU, 2010. A four-month flat shelf. Report after the close on 2010-02-09, so 2010-02-10 is the PEG day, up 8.5%.
The gap clears the shelf on 3.0x volume, closing at 0.95 of its range. Then two tight days, 0.3% deep.
Buy at market over the pause high, 48.93. Stop a few cents under the low, 48.20.
Failure mode: a close under the PEG-day low. Instead it ran ten weeks up the 10-day. We sell into a push.

walkthroughs.title: COCO, April 2026: a pre-open report and a big gap
steps: COCO, 2026. A report before the open on 2026-04-29 makes that day the PEG day: a 17.4% gap on 4.0x volume.
The day closes at 0.98 of its range, the strong close we want. Then a six-day flag, 5.1% deep, before the buy.
Buy at market over the pause high, 69.58. Stop a few cents under the low, 68.27, 1.9% away.
We sell part into the push within about two weeks, day 3 or later. The rest trails the 9 EMA.

questions.q: Which line describes the last day on this chart?
choices: An earnings gap with a strong close
A news gap with no report behind it
An earnings gap that fades by the close
A pullback to the 20 EMA after earnings
questions.answer: An earnings gap with a strong close
questions.why: An earnings gap with a strong close. The report is the catalyst, and the strong close shows buyers still wanted the stock at the end of the day. Stewie defines a Power Earnings Gap this way. He does not want a gap that reverses and closes red. A gap with no report is a News Gapper, which is a different setup.
questions.lesson_line: A PEG is an earnings gap that closes strong.

wrong.An earnings gap that fades by the close: A gap that gives the day back by the close is not a PEG. This day closed near its high.
wrong.A news gap with no report behind it: The gap needs a report. A headline gap with no report belongs to the News Gapper.
wrong.A pullback to the 20 EMA after earnings: A pullback comes days after the gap, in the pause. This chart ends on the gap day itself.

questions.simple: A PEG is an earnings gap that closes strong, because a strong close shows buyers held the gap all day.

deeper.trap: The trap is stopping at 'earnings gap'. Some earnings gaps fade by the close. Stewie says a gap that reverses and closes in the red is not a PEG candidate. The strong close is part of the definition.

reasons: a plain definition: Stewie's wording plus our card agree

questions.story: A company reported after the close the day before. The chart ends on the next session, which opened far above the prior close.

questions.q: The PEG day is the first regular session after the earnings report.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. It is the report day for a report before the open, and the next session for a report after the close.
questions.lesson_line: Find the report time first. That tells you which session is the PEG day.

questions.q: Each earnings gap stays open all day. Which day is not a Power Earnings Gap?
choices: Gap 10%, closes at 0.20 of its range
Gap 10%, ends at 0.95 of its range
Gap 10%, closes at 0.80 of range
Gap 10%, closes at 0.88 of range
questions.answer: Gap 10%, closes at 0.20 of its range
questions.why: A close at 0.20 of the range is a faded day. A faded PEG day is not a PEG. It can become a delayed-reaction watch. Stewie wants a close at or near the highs.
questions.lesson_line: A gap that fades to a weak close is not a PEG.

wrong.Gap 10%, ends at 0.95 of its range: 0.95 is a close at the high, the ideal PEG candle.
wrong.Gap 10%, closes at 0.88 of range: 0.88 also sits in the top quarter, a strong close.
wrong.Gap 10%, closes at 0.80 of range: 0.80 sits in the top quarter, a strong close.

questions.simple: A gap that fades to a weak close is not a PEG, because a PEG needs a strong close.

deeper.trap: An open gap is not the test. A gap can stay open all day and still fade into a weak close. A faded PEG day is a delayed-reaction watch, not a buy.

reasons: rests on the proposed faded-day rule held under D-039
fixed before: choices replaced at the first check

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On a PEG pause buy, the stop goes a few ___ under the pause low or the trigger day's low.
questions.answer: cents
questions.why: Cents. The stop sits a few cents under the pause low or the trigger day's low, not exactly on it.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the low.

questions.q: Stewie's gap-and-go usually starts in the after-hours session. We buy PEGs the same way.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Stewie's gap-and-go often starts after hours, but we buy only in regular hours, at market. The regular session shows what the stock does: does the gap hold, and where does the day close. After-hours trading cannot show that.
questions.lesson_line: Regular hours only. The gap-and-go is not ours.
questions.simple: False. We buy only in regular hours, because the regular session shows whether the gap holds and how the day closes.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook E57 and E58

questions.q: The app's market filter sets how much the account trades: Green, Yellow, Orange or Red. Which readings suit a PEG?
choices: Green or Yellow
Green only
Yellow or Orange
Orange or Red
questions.answer: Green or Yellow
questions.why: Green or Yellow. The market filter tells us how hard to trade. Green allows full risk, and Yellow means smaller and fewer positions. Orange allows A+ setups only, the cleanest by our judgment, and Red is mostly cash and shorts. Coming out of a correction it is often the recent earnings gappers that perform best, so those weeks suit this setup.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market first: Green or Yellow for PEGs.

wrong.Orange or Red: Orange is for A+ setups only, and Red is mostly cash and shorts.
wrong.Green only: Yellow works too. It just means smaller and fewer.
wrong.Yellow or Orange: Orange allows A+ setups only, so it is not a general go-ahead.

questions.simple: Green or Yellow, because those readings let the account take new longs, while Orange and Red cut risk back hard.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook F65 market readings

questions.q: Stewie calls a close at or near the highs of the session the ideal PEG candle.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Stewie: a candle that closes at or near the highs of the session is the most ideal Power Earnings Gap candidate. Our A grade is a close in the top quarter of the day's range.
questions.lesson_line: A close near the high is the ideal PEG candle.
questions.simple: Yes. A close at or near the high of the day makes the ideal PEG candle.

reasons: the top-quarter A grade is our proposed line, while Stewie's quote only says near the highs

questions.q: Where does an A-grade PEG day close?
choices: In the top quarter of its range
Anywhere above the open
Just above the prior close
Mid-range on heavy volume
questions.answer: In the top quarter of its range
questions.why: In the top quarter of its range. A close at or near the high is the ideal candle.
questions.lesson_line: A close near the high is the A grade.

wrong.Anywhere above the open: Above the open is not enough for the A grade.
wrong.Just above the prior close: A close that low has given most of the gap back.
wrong.Mid-range on heavy volume: Heavy volume does not fix a mid-range close.

questions.q: Before you buy, a slight undercut of the PEG-day low that closes back over it ends the PEG setup.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A dip under the PEG-day low that closes back over it means sellers tried and buyers took the stock back. Only a close under the low shows it has given way. So a slight undercut does not end the setup. Gap Support is a different thing: the later test of the gap-up low, days or weeks on.
questions.lesson_line: A slight undercut that reclaims is not a failure.
questions.simple: No. A dip that closes back above the low shows buyers defended it, so the setup stays on.

reasons: rests on our card alone, no web source

questions.q: Before you buy, which event ends the PEG setup?
choices: A daily close under the PEG-day low
A quiet day on lighter volume
A pullback to the 10-day
An inside day in the pause
questions.answer: A daily close under the PEG-day low
questions.why: A daily close under the PEG-day low. The gap-day low has given way on a close, so there is nothing to buy.
questions.lesson_line: A close under the PEG-day low ends it.

wrong.A quiet day on lighter volume: Quiet days on lighter volume are what a good pause looks like.
wrong.A pullback to the 10-day: A shallow pullback that holds the PEG-day low is still a pause.
wrong.An inside day in the pause: An inside day is one of the tight pauses we look for.

questions.q: Before a buy, a trade back to the prior close means the gap filled and the PEG is off.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Before a buy, a trade at or under the prior close means the gap filled, and the PEG is off. The test is any trade at that price, not only a close. Morpheus: any stock that fills the opening gap should be avoided.
questions.lesson_line: A filled gap is a dead PEG.
questions.simple: Yes. If price trades back to the prior close, the gap has filled and we pass.

reasons: the fill test is on our card and Morpheus agrees

questions.q: Which stock passes our liquidity rule?
choices: $25 and $50 million a day
$8 and $60 million a day
$40 and $12 million a day
$6 and $5 million a day
questions.answer: $25 and $50 million a day
questions.why: $25 and $50 million a day. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
questions.lesson_line: Ten dollars and twenty million a day, or we skip.

wrong.$40 and $12 million a day: The dollar volume is under $20 million a day.
wrong.$6 and $5 million a day: Both fail: price under $10 and volume under $20 million.

questions.q: Which session is the PEG day?
questions.story: The last bar on the chart is Tuesday's close. The company reports after that close. You check the earnings calendar that evening.
choices: Wednesday, next session
Tuesday, report day
Thursday, once settled
Friday, a pause forms
questions.answer: Wednesday, next session
questions.why: Wednesday. A report after the close cannot be traded until the next session, so Wednesday is the market's first real reaction and the PEG day. Only a report before the open makes the report day itself the PEG day. Check the report time first.
questions.lesson_line: After the close, the next session is the PEG day.

wrong.Tuesday, report day: Tuesday's regular session was over before the report.
wrong.Thursday, once settled: Waiting a day misses the reaction; the first session is the PEG day.
wrong.Friday, a pause forms: The pause comes after the PEG day, not before.

questions.simple: A report after Tuesday's close is first traded on Wednesday, so Wednesday is the PEG day.

deeper.example: AMZN reported on 2017-10-26 after the close, so its PEG day was 2017-10-27. BURL reported on 2016-05-26 before the open, so its PEG day was the report day, 2016-05-26. The report time decides which session counts.

reasons: rests on our setup card and dossier only

questions.q: Growing sales and earnings, a beat and a raise make a PEG stronger, but the chart still comes first.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Growing sales and earnings, a beat and ideally a raise make the gap more believable, so they raise the grade. A grade is our judgment of how clean the setup is, and it sets the size. The chart still comes first, because it shows what buyers actually do. The app cannot check the numbers for you.
questions.lesson_line: Strong numbers help the grade. The chart decides.
questions.simple: True. Strong numbers make the gap more believable, but the chart shows what buyers do, so it decides first.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook D40

questions.q: On a PEG you may add shares later if volume climbs after the buy.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. We size the shares from one price and one stop. An add changes both, so the risk is no longer what the plan set. A PEG is one buy at one price with one stop, with no adding and no starter position.
questions.lesson_line: One buy, one price, one stop. No adding.
questions.simple: False. The size is set from one price and one stop, and an add would break the risk the plan set.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A5

questions.q: Bought at 69.58 with the stop at 68.27. One R is the gap between them. Where is 3R?
questions.why: $73.51. One R is the fill minus the stop: 69.58 - 68.27. Add three of those to the fill: 69.58 + 3 x (69.58 - 68.27) = 73.51.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R price before the open.
questions.simple: Add three times the gap between the fill and the stop to the fill, which gives 73.51.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook B19 third at 3R
fixed before: the BIDU 27.7R claim was dropped

wrong.$72.20: Counted 3R up from the stop, which is only two R above the fill.
wrong.$72.58: Added three dollars to the fill. 3R is three times the risk, not three dollars.
wrong.$74.82: Added four R, one too many.

questions.story: The day of the pause break.

questions.q: The PEG day's low is 70.00, high 76.00, close 74.80. Where in the range did it close, from 0 to 1?
questions.why: 0.80. The close above the low is 74.80 - 70.00. The range is 76.00 - 70.00. So (74.80 - 70.00) / (76.00 - 70.00) = 0.80. Stewie wants a close at or near the highs, and 0.80 is in the top quarter. Our card cues that as an A, but grading is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: Close minus low, over the range. The top quarter is a strong close.
questions.simple: The close sits 0.80 of the way from the low to the high, which is inside the top quarter.

reasons: a computed key
the top-quarter A-grade close is proposed and held under D-039

wrong.0.98: Divided the close by the high. That ignores the low.
wrong.0.20: Measured down from the high instead of up from the low.
wrong.0.06: Divided by the close, not by the day's range.

questions.q: Where does the stop go on a PEG pause buy?
choices: A few cents under the pause low
At the prior close, the gap-fill price
Exactly on the pause low, no cushion
A fixed 5% under the fill
questions.answer: A few cents under the pause low
questions.why: A few cents under the pause low, or under the trigger day's low. That low is the nearest spot where the buy is clearly wrong, so the loss stays small. It is never wider than under the PEG-day low, because a close under that low ends the setup. The stop sits a few cents under a real low, not exactly on it.
questions.lesson_line: A few cents under a real low, never wider than the gap-day low.

wrong.At the prior close, the gap-fill price: The prior close is far below the pause. That is a much wider stop than the rule allows.
wrong.A fixed 5% under the fill: A fixed percentage ignores the chart. The stop sits under a real low.
wrong.Exactly on the pause low, no cushion: The stop sits a few cents under the low, not exactly on it.

questions.simple: A few cents under the pause low, because that is the nearest price where the buy is clearly wrong.

deeper.example: AMZN: the buy went in over the pause high at 56.14, and the stop went in at 55.39. The size then came from the distance between those two prices.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3 and F62

questions.q: A PEG in profit can be held through its next earnings report whatever the open gain.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Sell before the next report unless the trade is up 5R. Hold through a report only at 5R or better.
questions.lesson_line: Into the next report only with 5R in hand.

questions.q: What can you buy?
questions.story: The app's market filter turns Orange, which allows only A+ setups. You grade one PEG an A+ and the other a B-. A grade is our judgment of how clean the setup is.
choices: Only the A+ one; pass on the B-
Both, with the B- at half size
Neither; Orange means all cash
Both, with a wider stop on the B-
questions.answer: Only the A+ one; pass on the B-
questions.why: Only the A+ one. In an Orange market the filter allows A+ setups only, so the account stays out of trouble when the market is shaky. Only the cleanest setups get risk. Grading is a judgment call, so grade the setup honestly before you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Orange: A+ setups only.

wrong.Neither; Orange means all cash: Orange still allows an A+ setup. Red is the mostly-cash reading.
wrong.Both, with the B- at half size: Orange allows A+ setups only, not weaker ones at half size.
wrong.Both, with a wider stop on the B-: A wider stop does not make a B- an A+.

questions.simple: In Orange only the cleanest setups get risk, so only the one you grade A+ can be bought.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook F65 Orange reading

questions.q: How do we trail what is left of a PEG?
choices: A close under the 9 or 20 EMA
A single touch of the 50-day line
Holding until the next report
Selling at a fixed 10R target
questions.answer: A close under the 9 or 20 EMA
questions.why: Sell on a close under the 9 EMA for a fast mover, or under the 20 EMA for a steadier one. An EMA is an average of recent closes that rises with the trend, so a close under it is the first sign the run has slowed. It takes a close, not a touch, so one poke does not shake us out of a winner.
questions.lesson_line: Trail what is left under the 9 or 20 EMA.

wrong.Holding until the next report: Holding into a report needs 5R. It is not the trail.
wrong.Selling at a fixed 10R target: A fixed target is not a trail. The average decides.
wrong.A single touch of the 50-day line: The default trail is the 9 or 20 EMA, and it sells on a close, not a touch.

questions.simple: We sell what is left on a close under the 9 or 20 EMA, because that is the first sign the run has slowed.

deeper.example: BIDU, 2010: after a four-month flat shelf and two tight days, the stock ran ten weeks along its fast EMA.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook E52; the trail choice is held under D-024

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We usually wait until day ___ at the earliest for a first sell.
questions.why: 3. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: First sell: day 3 at the earliest, by judgment.
questions.simple: We wait until day 3 at the earliest for a first sell, and it is a judgment call.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B19 and E51

questions.q: Prior close 50.00, today's open 55.60. How big is the gap, in percent?
questions.why: 11.2%. The gap is the open minus the prior close, over the prior close: (55.60 - 50.00) / 50.00 = 11.2%. A gap of 10% or more is a strong cue on our card, a guide and not a rule.
questions.lesson_line: Gap percent is open over prior close. Ten percent is a strong cue.
questions.simple: The open is 11.2 percent above the prior close, which is over the 10 percent cue on our card.

reasons: a computed key
the 10% A cue is proposed and the gap floor is held under D-033

wrong.5.6%: Used the dollar gap as if it were the percent.
wrong.10.1%: Divided the gap by the open, not by the prior close.
wrong.1.1%: A decimal slip, one place too far left.

questions.q: Which trade is this?
questions.story: Three weeks after a PEG, the stock dips under the PEG-day low and closes back over it.
choices: Gap Support, the later test
A new PEG; buy it
A failed PEG; short it
A News Gapper
questions.answer: Gap Support, the later test
questions.why: Gap Support. A slight undercut of the gap-day low that closes back over it is not a PEG failure. The gap day is the PEG; the later test is Gap Support.
questions.lesson_line: The gap day is a PEG. The later test of its low is Gap Support.

wrong.A new PEG; buy it: A PEG is the report's reaction day and its first pause, not a test weeks later.
wrong.A failed PEG; short it: A close back over the low is not a failure, and we do not short a PEG.
wrong.A News Gapper: A News Gapper needs a headline that is not a report; this gap was earnings.

questions.q: Fill 90.25, stop 88.19. How far is the stop below the fill, in percent?
questions.why: 2.3%. The distance is the gap over the fill: (90.25 - 88.19) / 90.25 x 100 = 2.3%. We prefer a stop 1 to 3% away and accept up to 5%. A close stop keeps the loss small, and the same risk buys more shares. Past 5% we mostly wait for a tighter trigger. These are LULU's levels.
questions.lesson_line: Stop distance is the fill minus the stop, over the fill.
questions.simple: The stop sits 2.3 percent under the fill, inside the range we prefer, so the loss stays small.

reasons: a computed key
the stop range is the owner's ruling D-005

wrong.97.7%: Gave the stop as a share of the fill, not the gap between them.
wrong.23.0%: A decimal slip, one place too far right.
wrong.206.0%: Turned the dollar gap into a percent without dividing by the fill.

questions.story: The day of the pause break.

questions.q: What is the most you will pay for it?
questions.story: The pause high is 60.00. At 10:15 the stock trades 62.80.
questions.why: 62.40. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and 4% over 60.00 is 62.40. At 62.80 the stock is past it, so we pass. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays where it was, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Miss it rather than chase it. Four percent and done.

wrong.61.20: 61.20 is under the line, but the highest price we pay is 62.40.

questions.simple: We never pay more than 4% over the buy point, because paying more stretches the distance to the stop and shrinks the size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C28 no-chase line

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: A leader reports after the close and is up 12% in after-hours trading on huge volume. A chat room says to buy now.
choices: Wait for regular hours and the pause
Buy now with a limit order
Buy half now, half at the open
Buy now; it will gap higher
questions.answer: Wait for regular hours and the pause
questions.why: Wait. We never buy outside regular hours. The PEG day is the next regular session, and the buy comes later, off the pause.
questions.lesson_line: No after-hours buys. Wait for the regular session.

wrong.Buy now with a limit order: Entries are market orders in regular hours, not after-hours limits.
wrong.Buy half now, half at the open: Half an after-hours buy is still an after-hours buy.
wrong.Buy now; it will gap higher: A gap that is going higher can wait for the regular session.

questions.q: What is the setup now, and why?
questions.story: Four days after the gap, the stock closes under the PEG-day low. You have not bought yet.
choices: Off; the low gave way on a close
Off; the pause has become a drift
On; a dip under the low is a pause
On; the gap has not filled yet
questions.answer: Off; the low gave way on a close
questions.why: Off. The PEG-day low is the line buyers have to defend, and a daily close under it means they gave it up. That ends the setup before a buy, so there is nothing to buy. A slight undercut that closes back over the low is different and does not end it.
questions.lesson_line: A close under the gap-day low means no PEG.

wrong.Off; the pause has become a drift: A drift is a run of lower highs and lower lows. The story does not describe one, and the close under the low is what ends it.
wrong.On; a dip under the low is a pause: A slight undercut that closes back over the low is allowed. This one closed under it, so the setup is off.
wrong.On; the gap has not filled yet: Not filling is not enough. A daily close under the PEG-day low ends the setup before a buy.

questions.simple: Off. A close under the PEG-day low means buyers gave up the line, so there is no PEG to buy.

reasons: rests on our card alone; the close-under-low invalidation is proposed

questions.q: Where is the stop now?
questions.story: You bought at 30.00 with the stop at 29.40. A follow-up headline gaps it open at 29.10. The first 30-minute bar's low is 28.95.
choices: 28.95, first 30-minute low
29.10, sell at the open
29.40, wait for a reclaim
28.80, two R under the fill
questions.answer: 28.95, first 30-minute low
questions.why: 28.95. On a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop. The open of a gap is the noisiest print, and the first half hour shows where buyers and sellers settle. You are out only if that loss is past 2R. Here 2R under the 30.00 fill is 28.80, so 28.95 is inside it.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low decides.

wrong.29.10, sell at the open: The first 30-minute bar decides. It is not an automatic sale at the open.
wrong.29.40, wait for a reclaim: The old stop is gone once the gap trades through it.
wrong.28.80, two R under the fill: Two R is the ceiling, not a stop to place.

questions.simple: The first 30-minute low of 28.95 is the new stop, because the open is noisy and the loss from there is inside 2R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B20
the key is worked out from the story prices

questions.q: On a PEG the stop moves to breakeven as soon as the buy fills.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Breakeven is the point after which a trade must never again become a loser, so a trade has to earn it first. The stop moves to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. Until then it stays a few cents under the low.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes later, between 2R and 5R or at the first sell.
questions.simple: False. A trade has to earn breakeven first, so the stop moves up later, after the trade has worked.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B19

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: A PEG closed strong on Tuesday, near the top of its range. Four quiet days since have held above the PEG-day low. This morning the stock trades over the highest high of those four days.
choices: Buy at market; stop under the low
Wait for the close to confirm
Buy at the PEG-day high with a limit
Skip it; the gap is too old now
questions.answer: Buy at market; stop under the low
questions.why: Buy at market. The quiet days show sellers ran out of steam while the low held. A trade over the pause high shows buyers are back, so that is the trigger. The stop goes a few cents under the low. Nothing here says skip.
questions.lesson_line: Buy as price trades over the pause high.

wrong.Wait for the close to confirm: Waiting for the close hands away the trigger and the price.
wrong.Buy at the PEG-day high with a limit: A limit at the PEG-day high is not the trigger. The pause high is.
wrong.Skip it; the gap is too old now: The low is holding and nothing says skip.

questions.simple: Buy at market as price trades over the pause high, because that shows buyers are back after the quiet days.

deeper.example: LOGI, 2023: the PEG day was 2023-10-24. Four flat days made a pause 2.4% deep. The buy came on 2023-10-31 over the pause high at 78.20, with the stop at 77.34.

reasons: the pause buy as the default trigger is held under D-085

questions.q: PEG or News Gapper?
questions.story: A stock gaps 6.3% on 2.7x volume and closes at 96% of its range. The earnings calendar shows no report that day. The last one was five weeks ago.
choices: News Gapper; not a report day
PEG; the gap and close qualify
Episodic Pivot; any gap with volume
Kicker; it closed at the high
questions.answer: News Gapper; not a report day
questions.why: News Gapper. A PEG day is a report's reaction day. This gap came on a headline that was not a report, so it belongs to the News Gapper lesson.
questions.lesson_line: Check the earnings calendar. No report, no PEG.

wrong.PEG; the gap and close qualify: The close and volume are fine. The catalyst is what fails.
wrong.Episodic Pivot; any gap with volume: An Episodic Pivot needs a neglected name and a named surprise, not just volume.
wrong.Kicker; it closed at the high: A Kicker needs a weak red close the day before.

questions.q: PEG or High Volume Edge?
questions.story: The gap day is the last bar. A well-known company reports and gaps up 6.2%. Volume is 7.6x its average, its biggest in a year, and the day closes at 0.55 of its range. A High Volume Edge is a setup where record volume is the whole signal.
choices: A PEG; earnings on a known name
A High Volume Edge; a record
An Episodic Pivot; a big gap
A News Gapper; gapped on news
questions.answer: A PEG; earnings on a known name
questions.why: A PEG. A report on an established name is the catalyst, so this stays a PEG even at a one-year volume record. Volume raises the grade. It is the setup itself only in a High Volume Edge, a record that dwarfs every prior day, usually on a lesser-known name. ASML at 7.6x was still just a PEG.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings on a known name stays a PEG, even on record volume.

wrong.A High Volume Edge; a record: An HVE dwarfs every prior day, usually on a lesser-known name.
wrong.An Episodic Pivot; a big gap: An Episodic Pivot is a neglected name, flat or down for six months. This one is well known.
wrong.A News Gapper; gapped on news: A News Gapper's gap comes on a headline that is not a report. This gap came with a report.

questions.simple: It is a PEG. The report is the catalyst, and volume only raises the grade unless volume itself is the setup.

deeper.counter: Volume alone does not make an HVE. An HVE is usually a lesser-known name. ASML at 7.6x was still a PEG, because the catalyst was a report on an established name. A record that dwarfs every prior day on a lesser-known name is the HVE case.

reasons: rests on our card alone
the split depends on the name, a judgment call

questions.q: PEG or Kicker?
questions.story: Monday ends with a weak red close. Tuesday opens 2% higher with no earnings and no headline, on light volume.
choices: A Kicker; weak close, small gap
A PEG; every gap up counts as one
A News Gapper; the gap is news
An Episodic Pivot; a weak close
questions.answer: A Kicker; weak close, small gap
questions.why: A Kicker. It needs a weak red close and a gap of 1.5% or more on positioning, rarely earnings. Monday closed weak and red, and Tuesday opened 2% higher with no report or headline. A PEG day is a report's reaction day. A News Gapper's gap comes on a headline that is not a report.
questions.lesson_line: A weak red close, then a small gap on no news, is a Kicker.

wrong.A PEG; every gap up counts as one: A PEG day is a report's reaction day. This gap had no earnings.
wrong.A News Gapper; the gap is news: A News Gapper's gap comes on a headline that is not a report. This one had no headline.
wrong.An Episodic Pivot; a weak close: An Episodic Pivot is a neglected name, flat or down for six months. The story gives no such history.

questions.simple: A Kicker. A weak red close followed by a small gap on no news is positioning, not earnings.

reasons: rests on our card alone
the Kicker gap floor is a card number

questions.q: PEG or Episodic Pivot?
questions.story: A stock nobody follows is down 20% over six months. It reports and gaps 15% on 5x volume.
choices: An Episodic Pivot; a neglected name
A PEG; it reported and then gapped up
A PEG; a gap of 15% is big enough
A News Gapper; the gap is the news
questions.answer: An Episodic Pivot; a neglected name
questions.why: An Episodic Pivot. A PEG is an established leader already working in a base or a quiet uptrend. An EP is a neglected name, flat or down for six months. That history is how we tell them apart, so the months before the report decide it, not the size of the gap.
questions.lesson_line: The six months before the report tell a PEG from an EP.

wrong.A PEG; it reported and then gapped up: A PEG comes from an established leader, not a forgotten name.
wrong.A PEG; a gap of 15% is big enough: Size does not decide it. The months before the report do.
wrong.A News Gapper; the gap is the news: A News Gapper's gap comes on a headline that is not a report. This gap came with a report.

questions.simple: It is an Episodic Pivot, because a neglected name that fell for six months is not an established leader.

reasons: the EP side rests on our card alone
SET.18 teaches the same split

questions.q: Grade the two.
questions.story: Two earnings gaps of 10% on 4x volume, both closing at the high. One comes out of a five-month base. The other follows a 45% run in three months.
choices: First stronger; second a B-
Both A+; the gap day is the same
Second stronger; strength builds
Both B-; a 10% gap is small
questions.answer: First stronger; second a B-
questions.why: First stronger, second a B-. For an A, the stock is not up more than 30% in the 65 sessions before the gap. The first gap came out of a five-month base. The second follows a 45% run in three months, which is a late gap and a B- cue. Both closed at the high, so the days look alike but the months before them do not.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet before the gap is an A cue. A late gap is a B-.

wrong.Both A+; the gap day is the same: The days look alike, but the months before them do not.
wrong.Second stronger; strength builds: A big run into the report is the late-gap warning, not a plus.
wrong.Both B-; a 10% gap is small: A gap of 10% or more is an A-grade cue, not a small one.

questions.simple: The first gap is stronger. A late gap after a big run, like the 45% climb, grades B-.

deeper.trap: A 45% run in three months is well past the 30% line. A gap out of a five-month base is the opposite: price was quiet, so the gap is the first move. The two gap days can look identical on the chart.

reasons: the 30% run-up line is a proposed number on our card
rests on our card alone

questions.q: Grade each pause.
questions.story: Two pauses follow the same kind of gap. One is three tight days on lighter volume that hold the PEG-day close. The other is seven loose days that dip under the PEG-day low before closing back over it.
choices: First an A+ cue; second a B-
Both the same; the gap decides
First a B-; lighter volume is weak
Second an A+; it dipped and held
questions.answer: First an A+ cue; second a B-
questions.why: First an A+ cue, second a B-. A tight pause on lighter volume that holds the PEG-day close is an A+ cue. A loose, deep pause that undercuts the PEG-day low is a B- cue. Both pauses follow the same kind of gap, so the pause itself sets the grade.
questions.lesson_line: Tight and holding is A+. Loose and deep is a B-.

wrong.Both the same; the gap decides: The pause is graded on its own, and these two are very different.
wrong.First a B-; lighter volume is weak: A tight pause on lighter volume that holds the PEG-day close is an A+ cue.
wrong.Second an A+; it dipped and held: A loose, deep pause that undercuts the PEG-day low is a B- cue, even when it closes back over.

questions.simple: The tight pause that holds the close is an A+ cue. The loose, deep one is a B-.

reasons: both grading cues are on our card alone

questions.q: A PEG still under 1R after 10 trading days is held while the stop has not been hit.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, even if the stop has not been hit. It frees the money for a better trade. The time stop does not apply to a trade already at 1R or more.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days under 1R and we sell.
questions.simple: No. If a trade is still under 1R after 10 trading days, we sell it even though the stop has not been hit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: How do you handle the first sell?
questions.story: You bought at 40.00 with the stop at 39.00, so 3R is 43.00. It is day 2 of the hold, and the stock opens at 43.60.
choices: Hold it all; judge it from day 3
Sell a third at the open, 43.60
Sell a third at the close
Sell half, since it gapped up
questions.answer: Hold it all; judge it from day 3
questions.why: Hold it all. We very rarely sell on day 1 and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. Here the open of 43.60 is past 3R at 43.00, but it is only day 2. The measured edge comes from the few big runs, so selling too soon cuts the part that pays.
questions.lesson_line: Past 3R on day 2 is not a sell signal. Day 3 at the earliest.

wrong.Sell a third at the close: Selling at the close on day 2 is still early. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest.
wrong.Sell half, since it gapped up: Half is still a fixed early sell. We wait until day 3 at the earliest and judge the push.
wrong.Sell a third at the open, 43.60: A fixed third at 3R is not our rule. The first sell is a judgment, and we usually wait until day 3.

questions.simple: Hold. The first sell is a judgment, and selling too soon cuts the big runs that pay for the plan.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63 and the 3R trim)

questions.q: Account 50,000. Risk 0.5%. Fill 90.25, stop 88.19. How many shares?
questions.answer: 121 shares
questions.why: 121 shares. Dollars at risk are 50,000 x 0.5%. Risk per share is the fill minus the stop: 90.25 - 88.19. Divide the first by the second and round down to 121. Sizing from the stop means a stop-out costs the planned amount whatever the price. The position cap can only make it smaller.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: The risk dollars divided by the distance to the stop gives 121 shares, so a stop-out costs only the planned amount.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook A3 and A5
fixed before: risk cut to 0.5% to stay under the cap

choices: 109 shares
554 shares
121 shares
1,213 shares

wrong.554 shares: Divided the account by the price and ignored the stop.
wrong.1,213 shares: Typed the risk as ten times too big, so the share count came out ten times too big.
wrong.109 shares: Divided the risk dollars by the stop's percent, not by the dollars per share.

questions.story: The day of the pause break.

questions.q: Keep the stop or tighten it for size?
questions.story: The pause high is 61.00 and the pause low is 59.30. The honest stop, a few cents under the low, is about 2.9% from the fill. A friend says to put the stop at 60.10 so the size can be bigger.
choices: Keep the stop; let it set the size
Put the stop at 60.10 to fit more
Buy the bigger size, same stop
Split the buy in two to cut risk
questions.answer: Keep the stop; let it set the size
questions.why: Keep the stop and let it set the size. The stop goes first, a few cents under the pause low, and the size comes from it. You never pick a size and then back-fit a stop inside the noise. Here the honest stop is about 2.9% from the fill. If it does not fit the risk budget, skip the trade rather than tighten the stop.
questions.lesson_line: If the honest stop does not fit, size down or skip.

wrong.Split the buy in two to cut risk: A PEG is one buy at one price with one stop. No adding and no starter position.
wrong.Put the stop at 60.10 to fit more: Pulling the stop in to get more shares is the mistake, not the plan.
wrong.Buy the bigger size, same stop: A bigger size on this stop risks more than the plan allows.

questions.simple: Keep the stop, because the stop marks where the buy is wrong and the size comes from it, never the other way round.

deeper.trap: The trap is working backward: pick the size you want, then move the stop to fit. The order is stop first, then size. Here the honest stop is wider than the friend's tight stop, so the formula gives fewer shares. If even that does not fit the risk, skip the trade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A5)
stop width kept inside the usual 3% so the open stop-cap decision (D-005) does not touch the key

questions.q: Hold or sell?
questions.story: You are up 3.5R on a PEG, bought two weeks ago. The next report is in two sessions.
choices: Sell it before the report
Hold; last report was a winner
Sell half now, hold the rest
Hold; the stop protects you
questions.answer: Sell it before the report
questions.why: Sell before the report. We hold through a report only when the trade is up 5R, and 3.5R is under that line. A stop cannot catch an overnight gap, so a report can take the stock far past it. A trade has to build a cushion before it can carry that risk.
questions.lesson_line: Under 5R going into a report, sell first.

wrong.Hold; last report was a winner: The last report says nothing about the next one.
wrong.Sell half now, hold the rest: The part still held would sit through the report, and the trade is under 5R.
wrong.Hold; the stop protects you: A stop does not protect against a gap through it.

questions.simple: Sell before the report, because a stop cannot catch an overnight gap and this trade has not built the cushion yet.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought a PEG pause break. Ten trading days later it sits at 0.4R, never near 3R and never near the stop.
choices: Sell it all and free the money
Sell half and keep half running
Hold; the stop has not been hit yet
Move the stop to breakeven and wait
questions.answer: Sell it all and free the money
questions.why: Sell. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, even though the stop has not been hit. At 0.4R it is tying up money a better trade could use, and selling frees it. Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, not at 0.4R.
questions.lesson_line: A slow PEG under 1R gets sold on day ten.

wrong.Hold; the stop has not been hit yet: The time stop exists for exactly this trade.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven and wait: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R. This trade is at 0.4R.
wrong.Sell half and keep half running: The time stop sells the trade. Half held is still a trade under 1R after 10 days.

questions.simple: Sell. A trade this slow ties up money a better trade could use, so the time stop frees it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: How do you start?
questions.story: A correction just ended and the app's market filter turned Green, which allows full risk. It is earnings season, and six leaders gapped on reports this week.
choices: A few positions; more as they work
Three now, three more tomorrow
All six; Green means full risk
None; wait for a second Green week
questions.answer: A few positions; more as they work
questions.why: A few positions, adding more positions as the first ones work. A turn to Green can still be a false start, and six new positions at once would put six stops at risk together. A few that work show the turn is real. This is also the season where the recent earnings gappers often lead.
questions.lesson_line: After a correction, start with a few positions and add more as they work.

wrong.None; wait for a second Green week: Waiting gives up the first earnings season after a correction, which this setup favors.
wrong.Three now, three more tomorrow: Adds follow how the first ones work, not the calendar.
wrong.All six; Green means full risk: Start with a few and add only as the first ones work.

questions.simple: Start with a few positions, because if the turn fails you lose on fewer, and add more as the first ones work.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook F68
fixed before: the best-time overclaim was softened

questions.q: Take the pause break, and why?
questions.story: A $24 stock trades about $12 million a day. It gaps 14% on earnings on 6x volume, closes at the high, and sets up a perfect pause.
choices: No; under $20 million a day
Yes; the gap day's volume is huge
No; a 14% gap is too big to chase
Yes, but only at half the size
questions.answer: No; under $20 million a day
questions.why: No. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. That floor lets us get in and out without pushing the price. The $24 price passes, but about $12 million a day fails. One huge gap day does not count, because the test is the usual dollar volume before the gap.
questions.lesson_line: Liquidity first: $10 and $20 million a day.

wrong.Yes; the gap day's volume is huge: The rule is about the usual dollar volume before the gap, not one big day.
wrong.No; a 14% gap is too big to chase: The no-chase rule is about the buy point: never buy more than 4% above it. A big gap is not a ban.
wrong.Yes, but only at half the size: Half size does not fix a liquidity failure.

questions.simple: No. About $12 million a day is under our $20 million floor, so we could not get in and out cleanly.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: PEGs bunch into four earnings seasons a year, one for each quarterly report.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Companies report every quarter, and most report in the same few weeks, so PEG chances bunch into four earnings seasons a year. A list of leaders kept for each season has the names ready when they report.
questions.lesson_line: Four earnings seasons a year, so four windows for the setup.
questions.simple: True. Companies report each quarter in a few busy weeks, so PEGs bunch into four seasons and a list has the names ready.

reasons: one cited fact only, from our own setup card

questions.q: A $60 stock averages 400,000 shares a day. What is the most you should own?
questions.answer: 4,000 shares
questions.why: 4,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 400,000 / 100 = 4,000. A bigger position cannot be sold quickly without pushing the price. This is a ceiling, and the risk-based size may be smaller.
questions.lesson_line: Never more than one percent of a day's average volume.
questions.simple: One percent of 400,000 shares a day is 4,000, the most we hold, so we can sell out without moving the price.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook D42

choices: 4,000 shares
40,000 shares
8,000 shares
400,000 shares

wrong.40,000 shares: Took ten times the right share of the volume.
wrong.8,000 shares: Doubled the 1% rule. The ceiling is 1% of the average daily volume.
wrong.400,000 shares: Used the whole average daily volume as the limit.

questions.q: What did that loss pay for?
questions.story: NVDA, 2024. A PEG gapped 11.2% on 1.9x volume and closed at 0.99 of its range, after a 36% run in 65 sessions. You bought the pause break and the stop went that week.
choices: A late gap after a big run
A report with no beat
A buy made after hours
A stop set too wide
questions.answer: A late gap after a big run
questions.why: A late gap after a big run. The 36% run before the report was past the 30% A-grade cue. The loss was a planned one-R loss.
questions.lesson_line: A big run into the report is a warning even on a perfect gap.

wrong.A report with no beat: Nothing in the story says the report missed.
wrong.A buy made after hours: The buy came on a gap open in regular hours.
wrong.A stop set too wide: The stop was only 0.5% away, which is tight, not wide.

questions.q: What was that loss?
questions.story: A 10.6% earnings gap on 7.5x volume closed 61% of the way up its range, where 100% is the high. After the pause you bought the break at 45.07 with the stop at 43.78, 2.9% away. It went straight to the stop.
choices: A weaker setup the stop capped
A mistake; the stop was too tight
A mistake; the volume was too heavy
Bad luck; nothing in the chart
questions.answer: A weaker setup the stop capped
questions.why: A weaker setup the stop capped. The gap day closed 61% of the way up its range. Stewie calls a close at or near the highs the ideal PEG candle, so this close was weaker than ideal and the setup less clean. The 2.9% stop is inside our 1 to 3% preference, so it was not too tight. Heavy volume is not the flaw. The stop did its job and the loss stayed small.
questions.lesson_line: A close short of the high makes a weaker trade. The stop capped the loss.

wrong.A mistake; the stop was too tight: A 2.9% stop is inside our 1 to 3% preference. It was not too tight.
wrong.A mistake; the volume was too heavy: Volume raises the grade. Heavy volume is not a flaw, and 7.5x is not the problem.
wrong.Bad luck; nothing in the chart: The close at 61% of the range was weaker than the near-the-high close Stewie wants, so the chart did show something.

questions.simple: A weaker setup that the stop capped. The close was well short of the high, so the setup was less clean.

deeper.trap: The trap is hunting for blame in a stopped trade. CELH had one small warning before the buy: a close only 61% of the way up its range. The stop still kept the loss small, which is what stop first is for.

reasons: the example is read off our own bars, not a published source
the weak-close reading rests on Stewie's ideal-candle line, not a rule

questions.q: Was that a mistake?
questions.story: A 10.7% gap on 4.6x volume, close at 0.98, then a clean pause. You bought the eighth-day break at 107.16 with the stop at 104.36, 2.6% away. It never reached 1R and the stop traded.
choices: A planned loss; the stop worked
A mistake; the PEG should be skipped
A planned loss, so widen the stop
A mistake; buy on day one instead
questions.answer: A planned loss; the stop worked
questions.why: No. A textbook gap and a textbook pause still lost. We size by the stop, so a loss at the stop is about 1R and the plan keeps working. In our scan of past PEGs, 31.0% reached 3R before the stop and 20.0% reached 5R. A trade can pass every test and still lose, so we judge the plan across many trades.
questions.lesson_line: Every gate can pass and the stop can still go.

wrong.A mistake; the PEG should be skipped: Nothing in the story fails a test. Skipping a clean setup is not a plan.
wrong.A planned loss, so widen the stop: Calling it planned is right, but the stop comes from the chart, and a wider one only shrinks the size.
wrong.A mistake; buy on day one instead: Nothing says day one would have done better.

questions.simple: It was a planned loss. Every test passed and the stop kept the loss to about 1R, so the system worked.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging a trade by its result. ELF passed every gate and still stopped out before 1R. In our scan only 31.0% reached 3R before the stop, so most hits did not get there. Judge the plan across many trades, not this one.

reasons: the base rate is a scan of our own bars, survivor-biased, not a published statistic
rests on the dossier alone for the example

questions.q: How does this PEG grade?
questions.story: A mega-cap that dozens of analysts follow. It gaps 5.4% on earnings on 3.8x volume and closes at 0.89 of its range. Two quiet days then hold above the gap-day low. A grade is our judgment of how clean the setup is.
choices: B-; many analysts follow it
A+; a clean pause beats it
A; large names hold up
No trade; too well known
questions.answer: B-; many analysts follow it
questions.why: B-. Bonde found that earnings breakouts on companies with significant analyst coverage do not do as well. A clean pause helps, but it does not lift the grade past that. A mega-cap can still be a PEG; it just grades lower. Grading is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: A widely covered mega-cap grades lower.

wrong.A+; a clean pause beats it: A clean pause helps, but a mega-cap with many analysts still grades lower. The pause does not lift it.
wrong.A; large names hold up: Bonde: earnings breakouts on companies with significant analyst coverage do not do as well.
wrong.No trade; too well known: A mega-cap can still be a PEG; it just grades lower.

questions.simple: It grades B-, because Bonde found earnings breakouts on widely covered companies do not do as well.

deeper.counter: Not every big name is a pass. A covered mega-cap grades lower, but it is not a no trade. Bonde says earnings breakouts on companies with significant analyst coverage do not do as well as the first kinds. So the grade drops, not the label.

reasons: the B- catalyst cue is on our card (proposed)
Bonde's line is general, not about PEGs by name

questions.q: Bought at 61.35, stop 60.21. A third sells at 67.05. How many R is that?
questions.why: 5R. One R is the fill minus the stop: 61.35 - 60.21. The gain per share is the sale minus the fill: 67.05 - 61.35. So (67.05 - 61.35) / (61.35 - 60.21) = 5.0, and that third banks 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Count every exit in R. The second third is 5R.
questions.simple: The sale is five times the fill-to-stop gap above the fill, so it is 5R.

deeper.example: ILMN: 6.5x volume out of a tight uptrend, then a three-day pause 3.2% deep that held the PEG-day close. It reached 3R in 5 sessions.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook E51 second third at 5R

wrong.0.2R: Flipped the division: one R over the gain.
wrong.1.1R: That is the risk per share read as R. Divide the gain by it.
wrong.0.1R: Divided the gain by the price, not by R.

questions.story: The day of the pause break.

questions.q: Do you buy the break, and why?
questions.story: The app's market filter reads Red. A leader gaps 12% on earnings on 5x volume, closes at the high, and sets up a tight pause.
choices: No; Red is mostly cash and shorts
No; a 12% gap is far too big to chase
Yes; a leader beats the market
Yes, but only at a smaller size
questions.answer: No; Red is mostly cash and shorts
questions.why: No. At a Red reading we are mostly in cash and short, so a new PEG long waits. The filter is a guide that keeps the account out of longs when the market is against them, and cash is a position. A perfect gap and a tight pause do not override it. Wait for the reading to turn Green or Yellow.
questions.lesson_line: Red market: mostly cash and shorts, so the PEG waits.

wrong.No; a 12% gap is far too big to chase: The no-chase rule is about the buy point: never buy more than 4% above it. A big gap is not a ban.
wrong.Yes; a leader beats the market: The reading is a guide for every long, leaders included.
wrong.Yes, but only at a smaller size: Smaller and fewer is the Yellow reading. Red is mostly cash and shorts.

questions.simple: No. In Red the filter says mostly cash, because even a great leader can fall with the market.

deeper.trap: The trap is 'great stocks ignore the market'. The reading is a guide for every long, leaders included. In Red the plan is mostly cash and shorts. At Orange only an A+ setup qualifies, and at Yellow the size is smaller and fewer.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)

questions.q: A loss taken at the stop on a valid PEG is a mistake.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A loss at the stop on a valid setup is the plan working. The scan found 31.0% reach 3R and 20.0% reach 5R before the stop.
questions.lesson_line: A loss at the stop is the system working.

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first trim.
questions.story: AMZN, 2017. A 5.5x volume gap closed at 0.92. Five flat days later it trades over the pause high of 56.14. The stop goes at 55.39.
choices: Market 56.14; stop 55.39; third at 58.39
Limit 54.00; stop 50.00; hold
Market at close; stop 56.14; 2R
Market 56.14; no stop; third at 10R
questions.answer: Market 56.14; stop 55.39; third at 58.39
questions.why: Market 56.14, stop 55.39, a third at 58.39. One R is the fill minus the stop; three of those above the fill is 58.39. AMZN reached 3R in 13 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop and first trim, written before the open.

wrong.Limit 54.00; stop 50.00; hold: A limit far below the market never fills, and a stop that wide breaks the size rule.
wrong.Market at close; stop 56.14; 2R: A stop at the entry is no stop, and the first trim is 3R.
wrong.Market 56.14; no stop; third at 10R: A real stop goes in with the broker, and the first third is at 3R.

questions.q: What is the read, and why?
questions.story: On day four of the pause, before you have bought, the stock trades back to the prior close at 11:00. It then rallies and closes above the PEG-day low.
choices: The gap filled; the setup is off
Off; the pause is drifting lower
Still on; the close is what counts
A Gap Support; buy the close
questions.answer: The gap filled; the setup is off
questions.why: The gap filled; the setup is off. Before a buy, a trade at or under the prior close means the whole gap has been erased. That holds even if the stock recovers and closes above the PEG-day low. Morpheus says any stock that fills the opening gap should be avoided.
questions.lesson_line: A trade back to the prior close fills the gap, even if it recovers.

wrong.A Gap Support; buy the close: Gap Support is the later test of the gap-up low. A trade all the way back to the prior close is a fill, not a test.
wrong.Off; the pause is drifting lower: A drift is a run of lower highs and lower lows. This is day four and the stock rallied.
wrong.Still on; the close is what counts: The fill test is a trade at or under the prior close, not a close.

questions.simple: The gap filled, so the setup is off, because the whole move of the gap was erased even though the day closed strong.

deeper.trap: The trap is the close. A daily-close check misses an intraday fill. The test is any trade at or under the prior close before you buy. A close back above the PEG-day low does not undo it.

reasons: the gap-fill test is a proposed card rule
'even if it recovers by the close' is our reading of a trade at or under the prior close

questions.q: How do you answer your friend?
questions.story: You bought the pause break with the stop a few cents under the pause low. The next day it dips toward the stop. A friend says to move the stop down to the gap-day low to give it room.
choices: Leave the stop where it is
Drop it to the gap-day low
Cancel it and watch it by hand
Buy more to lower your cost
questions.answer: Leave the stop where it is
questions.why: Leave the stop where it is. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. A stop that moves down turns a planned small loss into an open-ended one. The one exception is a gap through the stop, when the first 30-minute low becomes the new stop.
questions.lesson_line: The stop never moves down or wider.

wrong.Drop it to the gap-day low: The stop only moves up, never down or wider. Dropping it to the gap-day low widens it.
wrong.Cancel it and watch it by hand: The stop is the exit. Cancelling it removes the exit.
wrong.Buy more to lower your cost: A PEG is one buy at one price with one stop. No adding.

questions.simple: Leave it, because a stop that moves down turns the small loss we planned into an open-ended one.

deeper.trap: The trap is 'room'. A stop that moves down turns a planned small loss into an open-ended one. The only exception is a gap through the stop. Even then the first 30-minute low is the new stop, with a ceiling: if that takes the loss past 2R, get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)

questions.q: Is it a PEG?
questions.story: The gap day is the last bar. It gaps 11.2% on earnings on 2.7x volume. The day's low stays above the prior close of 116.78, but it closes at 0.23 of its range.
choices: No; it faded into a weak close
Yes; the gap held all day
Yes; the day is Gap Support
No; the gap filled by close
questions.answer: No; it faded into a weak close
questions.why: No. The gap held, since the low stayed above the prior close of 116.78, but the day faded and closed at 0.23 of its range. A close near the low means sellers took back the day, and Stewie does not want a gap that reverses. A faded day is not a PEG. It can become a delayed-reaction watch, but it is not a buy.
questions.lesson_line: A gap that fades is a watch, not a buy.

wrong.Yes; the gap held all day: Holding the gap is not enough. A faded PEG day is not a PEG.
wrong.Yes; the day is Gap Support: The gap day itself is never Gap Support. That is a later test of the gap-up low, days or weeks on.
wrong.No; the gap filled by close: The low stayed above the prior close, so the gap did not fill.

questions.simple: No. The gap stayed open, but the day closed near its low, so sellers won the day and it is not a PEG.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading 'gap still open' as strength. This stock kept its gap, with the low above the prior close, yet closed at 0.23 of its range. Buyers did not hold the move. A PEG needs the gap to hold and the close to be strong.

reasons: the faded-day line is proposed (D-039), but this close sits under every option

questions.q: Do you buy this one, and why?
questions.story: A stock has run 120% in a year and everyone is talking about it. It gaps 9% on earnings and closes at the high on huge volume.
choices: No; it is an exhaustion gap
No; the volume is too heavy
Yes; an A+ given the huge volume
Yes, on day one at the open
questions.answer: No; it is an exhaustion gap
questions.why: No. Treating an exhaustion gap after a huge run as a PEG is a named mistake. Bonde says that when the grandma in Timbuktu gets excited about it, it is an exhaustion gap. By then the news is widely known. The months before the report decide it, not the gap day.
questions.lesson_line: A gap after a huge run, with everyone talking about it, is not a PEG.

wrong.No; the volume is too heavy: Volume raises the grade; it does not fail a setup. The problem is the huge run before the gap.
wrong.Yes; an A+ given the huge volume: Huge volume does not offset a late gap after a huge run.
wrong.Yes, on day one at the open: This is an exhaustion gap, not a PEG, so there is no PEG buy on any day.

questions.simple: No. A stock everyone is talking about after a 120% run is an exhaustion gap, because the news is already widely known.

deeper.trap: The trap is that the day looks perfect: a gap, a close at the high, huge volume. The months before it decide. A 120% run that everyone talks about is Bonde's exhaustion gap. A quiet base before the gap is the better setup.

reasons: 'a huge run' is a judgment call; the 30% run cue is proposed
Bonde's line is a metaphor, backed by our card

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought at 50.00 with the stop at 49.00. News gaps it open at 47.40, and the first 30-minute bar's low is 47.20.
choices: Get out; the loss is past 2R
Stop at 47.20 and wait
Stop at 49.00; it will bounce
Sell half now and keep half
questions.answer: Get out; the loss is past 2R
questions.why: Get out. On a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop. But if that puts the loss past 2R, you are out. Here 47.20 is past 2R under the 50.00 fill. A planned loss is only the risk we sized for, so this is already far worse, and waiting only risks more.
questions.lesson_line: Past 2R in the first half hour, get out.

wrong.Stop at 47.20 and wait: The first 30-minute low is the new stop only while the loss is within 2R.
wrong.Stop at 49.00; it will bounce: The old stop is gone, and waiting for a bounce is hope.
wrong.Sell half now and keep half: Past 2R the rule says out, not half.

questions.simple: Get out, because the first 30-minute low of 47.20 puts the loss past 2R, far worse than the loss we planned.

deeper.trap: Do not wait for a bounce to the old 49.00 stop. A gap through the stop cancels that level. The first half hour sets the new stop, and past 2R we are out, not hoping.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B20 with its 2R ceiling
the key is worked out from the story prices

questions.q: Why does the plan still work?
questions.story: In our scan of 1,516 past PEG setups, 31.0% reached 3R and 20.0% reached 5R before the stop. Most never reached 3R.
choices: Small losses and a few big runs
A wider stop that rarely hits
A filter lifting wins to 80%
Holding winners into reports
questions.answer: Small losses and a few big runs
questions.why: Small losses and a few big runs. In that scan 31.0% reached 3R and 20.0% reached 5R before the stop. The measured edge comes from the few big runs, so we do not sell them too early. It is a scan of past bars, not a promise.
questions.lesson_line: Most buys stop short of 3R. The few big runs pay for them.

wrong.A wider stop that rarely hits: Our stops stay tight. A stop only moves up, never wider.
wrong.A filter lifting wins to 80%: The plan does not need a high win rate. It pays on the few big runs.
wrong.Holding winners into reports: Holding into a report needs 5R. The plan sells into strength instead.

questions.simple: Most buys never reach 3R, but the few that run far pay for the losses, so the plan can still work.

deeper.trap: Do not read 31.0% as a win rate. It is only the share that reached 3R before the stop, and 20.0% reached 5R. Most trades never reach 3R. The plan pays on the few runs, so we do not sell them too early.

reasons: a scan number that changes if the scan is re-run
fixed before: the worth-trading promise was removed

questions.q: Which day is the PEG day?
choices: The gap day, not a test weeks later
The day price tests the gap-up low
Any day above the gap-day high
The day the report is scheduled
questions.answer: The gap day, not a test weeks later
questions.why: The gap day, not a test weeks later. The gap day itself is just a PEG, never Gap Support. The later test of the gap-up low is Gap Support.
questions.lesson_line: The gap day is the PEG. The later test is Gap Support.

wrong.The day price tests the gap-up low: That later test is Gap Support.
wrong.Any day above the gap-day high: Staying above the gap-day high is not the reaction day.
wrong.The day the report is scheduled: The scheduled day is the report. The reaction day is the first regular session after it.

questions.q: Which one gets the bigger size?
questions.story: The app's market filter reads Yellow, which means smaller and fewer positions. You grade one PEG an A and the other a B-. A grade is our judgment of how clean the setup is, and it sets the size.
choices: The A; the B- is sized down
The B-; it has more room to run
Both the same; Yellow sets the size
Neither; Yellow means all cash
questions.answer: The A; the B- is sized down
questions.why: The A gets the bigger size. The grade sets the size: an A gets normal size, and a B- or lower is sized down, risking 0.25% to 0.5% against 0.5% to 1% for an A. The setup we trust least risks least. Yellow already means smaller and fewer. Grading is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: Match size to the grade. A weaker setup gets smaller size.

wrong.Neither; Yellow means all cash: Yellow means smaller and fewer, not all cash. Red is the mostly-cash reading.
wrong.The B-; it has more room to run: A weaker setup is the one we trust least, so it risks less, not more.
wrong.Both the same; Yellow sets the size: Yellow cuts the size for both, and the grade then sizes the weaker one down further.

questions.simple: The A gets the bigger size, because the setup we trust least risks the least.

deeper.trap: Do not read Yellow as all cash. Yellow means smaller and fewer, so a strong PEG is still taken, only smaller than in Green. Within that, the grade sets the size: A and B normal, A+ sized up, B- or lower sized down.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook D38 size by grade
fixed before: full size in Yellow was corrected

questions.q: Take the pause break once it triggers, or pass?
choices: Pass; it is under the 200-day
Take it; it fell far and looks cheap
Take it; the close is strong
Pass; the gap day closed weak
questions.answer: Pass; it is under the 200-day
questions.why: Pass. The gap-day close was under the 200-day, so this is a bear-market relief gap and there is no long. The close was 205.73 against a 200-day of 302.98, after a 42% fall over 65 sessions. Morales wants buyable gaps in an uptrend or a constructive base, not a downtrend. A big gap and a strong close do not lift a stock over that line.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, there is no long to buy.

wrong.Take it; the close is strong: A strong close under the 200-day is still under it.
wrong.Take it; it fell far and looks cheap: Cheap is not a trend. We take no longs below the 200-day simple moving average.
wrong.Pass; the gap day closed weak: The gap day closed at 0.82 of its range, a strong close. The problem is the 200-day, not the close.

questions.simple: Pass, because a stock under its 200-day is in a downtrend and a one-day gap does not change that.

deeper.counter: The candle was textbook and the trend was not. The gap was 16.0% on 3.1x volume and closed at 0.82 of its range. But the stock had fallen 42% over 65 sessions and sat far under its 200-day. The line decides before the candle does.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)
the 200-day value is read off our own bars
this question was fixed once before

questions.story: The chart ends on an earnings gap day. Check where the close sits against the 200-day line, the average of the last 200 closes.

questions.q: What is the call on this pause?
choices: Take it over the pause high
Take it now, before any break
Pass; the gap has been filled
Pass; the pause is drifting lower
questions.answer: Take it over the pause high
questions.why: Take it, on the break over the pause high. The gap held, because price never traded back to the prior close, and five quiet days stayed above the gap-day low. Sellers could not push it down. The trigger is a market buy as price trades over the pause high, 56.14 here, which came on 2017-11-06. A filled gap, a close under the gap-day low, or lower highs and lows would have taken it off.
questions.lesson_line: A gap that holds and a quiet pause are the setup.

wrong.Take it now, before any break: The plan buys as price trades over the pause high, not before.
wrong.Pass; the gap has been filled: The gap is still open; price never traded back to the prior close.
wrong.Pass; the pause is drifting lower: Five flat days are not a drift of lower highs and lower lows. The pause was only 1.7% deep.

questions.simple: Take it, but only as price trades over the pause high, because that shows buyers are back after the quiet days.

deeper.example: AMZN, October 2017: a report after the close on 2017-10-26 made 2017-10-27 the PEG day. Five flat days later the buy came over the pause high at 56.14 with the stop at 55.39. It reached 3R in 13 sessions, and our scan's best run on this trade was 24.7R.

reasons: the pause buy as the trigger is still open (D-085)
the key is read off our own bars, not a published source

questions.story: The chart ends five sessions after an earnings gap. Check whether price held the gap-day low and whether the gap has filled.

questions.q: A PEG day that opens up, fills the gap, then recovers into a strong close is still a valid PEG.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A trade back to the prior close fills the gap, and a filled gap ends the setup. Bulkowski and ChartSchool treat a breakaway gap as one that does not fill soon.
questions.lesson_line: A gap that fills is not a PEG, whatever the close.

questions.q: May you buy it again?
questions.story: Your PEG buy was stopped out on Tuesday, your first try on this stock this month. The PEG-day low still holds. By Friday the stock has formed a new pause and trades over its high.
choices: Yes; a new trigger is a new trade
No; one try per gap, then done
Yes; double size to recover
No; wait a week after a stop-out
questions.answer: Yes; a new trigger is a new trade
questions.why: Yes, on a new trigger. A stop-out says that entry failed, not that the setup is dead. If it triggers again, it is a new trade with its own stop and every rule. The limit is 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock. Doubling the size to win it back would break the sizing rule.
questions.lesson_line: After a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger.

wrong.Yes; double size to recover: Doubling size to win it back breaks the sizing rule.
wrong.No; one try per gap, then done: There is no one-try rule. There is a limit of tries a week and a month.
wrong.No; wait a week after a stop-out: The rule asks for a new trigger, not a waiting period.

questions.simple: Yes, because a stop-out ends one entry, not the setup, and a new trigger is a new trade with its own stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B21 and E56
fixed before: the revenge-trade wording was removed

questions.q: If you do buy at 85.60 on the gap day itself, where does the stop go?
questions.story: A leader gaps up on earnings from a prior close of 80.00. It opens at 84.80, dips to 83.60, then climbs to 85.60.
choices: A few cents under the 83.60 low
Just under the 84.80 open
The prior close, the gap line
Fixed 5% under the 85.60 fill

wrong.Just under the 84.80 open: The open is not the day's low. The stop goes under the low so far, 83.60.
wrong.The prior close, the gap line: The prior close, 80.00, is far under the day's low. The stop never goes wider than under that low.
wrong.Fixed 5% under the 85.60 fill: A fixed percentage ignores the chart. The stop sits under a real low.

questions.answer: A few cents under the 83.60 low
questions.why: A few cents under 83.60, the gap day's low so far. That low is the nearest price where this buy has clearly failed, so the stop goes just under it, never exactly on it. It is not under the 84.80 open, because the day already traded lower than that open.
questions.lesson_line: Day one: the stop sits a few cents under the low so far.
questions.simple: The stop goes a few cents under the day's low so far, 83.60, because that low is where this buy proves wrong.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook F62
fixed before: the day-one buy was made a conditional

questions.q: Gil Morales says a buyable gap-up should hold above the intraday low of the gap-up day.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Morales says a buyable gap-up should hold above the intraday low of the gap-up day, so that low is the selling guide. A gap that gives up its own low has shown sellers can overpower buyers. On day one our stop goes a few cents under the gap day's low so far. On a pause buy it goes a few cents under the pause or trigger-day low, never wider than under the gap-day low.
questions.lesson_line: The gap day's low is the line. A pause stop is never wider than a few cents under it.
questions.simple: Yes. The gap day's low is the line the stock should hold, because losing it shows sellers have taken over.

reasons: Morales is the only web source
the day-one stop wording is tied to the open day-one buy question

questions.q: What was the stock doing before this report?
questions.story: The chart ends on the gap day after the report. Check the four months before it.
choices: Moving sideways in a flat shelf
Running up 40% in three months
Sliding under its 200-day line
Falling steadily lower for months
questions.answer: Moving sideways in a flat shelf
questions.why: Moving sideways in a flat shelf. The stock sat in a four-month flat shelf, and the gap cleared it. Bonde wants stocks that have not rallied in anticipation of earnings. A quiet stock has not used up its move, so the gap is its first big step. A stock that already ran before the report is a late gap.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet base before the gap is the best setup. The gap is the first move.

wrong.Running up 40% in three months: This stock was quiet, not running. A big run before the report makes the gap late.
wrong.Sliding under its 200-day line: A slide under the 200-day would rule out a long. This stock sat in a flat shelf.
wrong.Falling steadily lower for months: The stock held its level for months. It was not in a steady fall.

questions.simple: A flat shelf. A stock that has not run before the report gets its first big move in the gap.

reasons: plain reading of our rulebook and the dossier's real example

questions.q: Which line describes the pause on this chart?
questions.story: The chart ends three sessions after an earnings gap day that closed in the upper part of its range. Check where the pause sits against the gap-day close and low.
choices: Tight days that hold the gap-day close
Drifting days under the gap-day low
A fill back to the prior close
A swing that undercuts the gap-day low
questions.answer: Tight days that hold the gap-day close
questions.why: Tight days that hold the gap-day close. The three days after the gap each closed above the gap-day close, in a narrow band, and stayed well above the gap-day low. Sellers could not push it down, so the buy over the pause high comes with a close stop. A drift, a gap fill or an undercut would each have taken the setup off or weakened it.
questions.lesson_line: A tight pause that holds the gap-day close shows sellers could not push it down.

wrong.Drifting days under the gap-day low: The pause stayed above the gap-day low. A drift would be lower highs and lows.
wrong.A fill back to the prior close: Price never traded back to the prior close. The gap stayed open.
wrong.A swing that undercuts the gap-day low: The pause stayed well above the gap-day low.

questions.simple: Tight days that hold the gap-day close show sellers could not push the stock down, so the stop can sit close.

reasons: plain reading of our rulebook and the dossier's real example

questions.q: Buy the close, wait for a pause or skip it?
questions.story: A leader gaps up on earnings and closes strong at 90.00. The day's low was 82.00. A friend says to buy the close with the stop under 82.00. That stop is almost 9% away.
choices: Wait for a pause; buy over its high
Buy the close; the setup is strong
Buy the close with a tighter 3% stop
Skip it; gaps this big never work
questions.answer: Wait for a pause; buy over its high
questions.why: Wait for a pause and buy over its high. We buy as price trades through a trigger during the day, never at the close. Buying the close puts the stop under the gap-day low, almost 9% away. We accept stops up to 5% and mostly wait for a tighter trigger past that. A pause brings the trigger and its low closer together. Never tighten the stop to fit.
questions.lesson_line: Do not buy the gap-day close. Wait for the pause and its trigger.

wrong.Buy the close; the setup is strong: A strong setup still needs a stop that fits. The close is the far end of the stop.
wrong.Buy the close with a tighter 3% stop: A stop pulled in to fit the size is not a real stop. It goes under a real low.
wrong.Skip it; gaps this big never work: The setup is fine. It just needs a trigger closer to its own low.

questions.simple: Wait for a pause, because buying the close puts the stop far away and a pause brings it close.

reasons: plain reading of our rulebook and the dossier's real example

questions.q: Sell, add or hold?
questions.story: You bought a PEG pause break at 40.00 with the stop at 39.00. On day 5 the stock has pushed up four days in a row and is up 6R, at 46.00.
choices: Sell part into the push; trail the rest
Sell all of it; 6R is plenty
Sell part, then add back on a dip
Sell nothing; wait for the next report
questions.answer: Sell part into the push; trail the rest
questions.why: Sell part into the push and trail the rest. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best. Kullamagi tells breakout traders to sell a third to a half after 3 to 5 days. A fast push is when buyers are plentiful, so part of the trade is banked. The rest stays, because the measured edge comes from the few big runs. We trail it under the 9 or 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some into the push, trail the rest.

wrong.Sell all of it; 6R is plenty: The plan pays on the few big runs, so we keep part for the trail.
wrong.Sell nothing; wait for the next report: We sell some into strength and trail the rest. Waiting for a report is not an exit plan.
wrong.Sell part, then add back on a dip: A PEG is one buy at one price with one stop. We never add, even after selling part.

questions.simple: Sell part into the strength and trail the rest, so you bank some and still keep the big runs.

reasons: plain reading of our rulebook and the dossier's real example
